questions.q: In Activity 10.1, a rubber band stretched across an open cardboard box is plucked. What happens to the sound once the rubber band stops vibrating?
o: The sound continues at the same loudness
questions.a: The sound stops: sound is produced only as long as the rubber band vibrates.

questions.q: A teacher uses a tuning fork, and not a hand clap, for most experiments with sound. Which reason fits the chapter?
o: A struck tuning fork gives a sound of nearly a single frequency
A tuning fork can produce sound without vibrating
The sound of a tuning fork can travel through vacuum
A tuning fork gives the loudest sound of any source
questions.a: A struck tuning fork gives a sound of nearly a single frequency, which makes it a simple, steady source to study; it still has to vibrate, and its sound still needs a medium.

questions.q:
Match each source of sound in column I with the part that vibrates in column II.
Column I: 1. A bansuri being blown  2. A cricket chirping  3. A person singing  4. A rubber band plucked across a box
Column II: (p) the vocal cords in the larynx  (q) the stretched band itself  (r) the air inside the hollow pipe  (s) the wings or legs rubbed together
questions.a: 1-r, 2-s, 3-p, 4-q: in a bansuri the air in the pipe vibrates, crickets rub their wings or legs, a singer's vocal cords vibrate, and a plucked rubber band vibrates itself.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Activity 10.2, a prong of the tuning fork is struck gently against a soft rubber pad, not against a hard surface.
Reason (R): An object can produce sound only when it is struck against something soft.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the activity does tell us to strike the fork on a rubber pad and not a hard surface, but sound is produced whenever an object vibrates, for example when a metal object is struck or a string is pulled.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by vibration? (b) What is the 'source' of a sound?
questions.a: (a) Vibration is the periodic to and fro motion (oscillation) of an object. (b) The source of a sound is the object that produces the sound.
s: (a) vibration is the periodic to and fro motion (oscillation) of an object
(b) the source is the object that produces the sound

questions.q: True or False: 'In most musical instruments, only one part vibrates to produce the sound.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. In most musical instruments more than one vibrating part is involved in producing sound; sound can come from vibrating strings, membranes and air columns together.
s: Verdict: False
Correct statement: most instruments have more than one vibrating part producing the sound

questions.q: Give a one-line reason for each. (a) Waves form on the water when a prong of a struck tuning fork touches it. (b) We feel a buzz when we gently touch our throat while talking. (c) A grasshopper can make sound even though it has no vocal cords.
questions.a: (a) The prong is vibrating, and its vibration disturbs the water surface. (b) The vocal cords inside the larynx vibrate to produce our voice. (c) Grasshoppers produce sound by rubbing their wings or legs, which makes them vibrate.
s: (a) the prong is vibrating and disturbs the water
(b) the vocal cords in the larynx vibrate while we talk
(c) it rubs its wings or legs to make them vibrate

questions.q: A school band has a sitar, a dholak (a drum with a stretched skin) and a bansuri. For each instrument, name the kind of part that vibrates to produce sound and what the player does to start the vibration.
questions.a: Sitar: its stretched strings vibrate; the player plucks them. Dholak: its stretched membrane (skin) vibrates; the player strikes it. Bansuri: the air column inside the hollow pipe vibrates; the player blows through it.
s: Sitar: strings vibrate, set going by plucking
Dholak: membrane vibrates, set going by striking
Bansuri: air column in the pipe vibrates, set going by blowing

questions.q: In a Class 9 laboratory in Jaipur, Ritu holds a steel tuning fork by its stem and strikes one prong gently on a rubber pad. She hears a steady hum when she brings it near her ear. When she dips the tip of one vibrating prong into a bowl of water, small waves spread across the surface. She strikes it again and holds it near her ear with the prongs pointing in different directions, and she still hears the hum each time. (a) Name the source of the sound she hears. (b) What do the waves on the water show? (c) Why does she hear the hum whichever way the prongs point? (d) A tuning fork makes sound with vibrating metal prongs. Name two other kinds of vibrating part that musical instruments use to produce sound.
questions.a: (a) The tuning fork, whose prongs are vibrating. (b) They show that the prongs are really vibrating, even though the motion is too fast to see. (c) Sound propagates in many directions from the source, so it reaches her ear in every orientation. (d) Any two of: vibrating strings (as in a sitar), vibrating membranes (as in a drum) and vibrating air columns (as in a bansuri).
s: (a) the tuning fork (its vibrating prongs) is the source
(b) the waves show the prongs are vibrating
(c) sound spreads in multiple directions from the source
(d) any two of strings, membranes and air columns

questions.q: A science museum is building a corner called 'Where does sound come from?' with four exhibits: (i) a taal (a pair of metal cymbals) that visitors strike together, (ii) a bansuri that visitors blow, (iii) a rubber band stretched across an open box that visitors pluck, and (iv) a sign asking visitors to touch their throat while they hum. For each exhibit, state what vibrates to produce the sound. Then decide which ONE exhibit best lets a visitor see that the sound stops as soon as the vibration stops, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (i) Taal: the metal itself vibrates when struck. (ii) Bansuri: the air inside the hollow pipe vibrates. (iii) Rubber band: the stretched band vibrates. (iv) Throat: the vocal cords inside the larynx vibrate. Best exhibit: the rubber band on the box. Its vibration can be watched directly, and the visitor can see that once the band stops vibrating the sound stops too; the air in the bansuri and the vocal cords cannot be seen, and the taal's vibration is hard to see.
s: (i) taal: the metal vibrates when struck
(ii) bansuri: the air in the hollow pipe vibrates
(iii) rubber band: the stretched band vibrates
(iv) throat: the vocal cords in the larynx vibrate
Decision: the rubber band, because its vibration is visible and the sound is seen to stop when it stops

questions.q: A space in which there is no medium (no matter) is called:
questions.a: A vacuum: a space where there is no medium, through which sound cannot propagate.

questions.q: At a swimming pool, Leena keeps her head under the water while her friend, also under the water, knocks two stones together. Leena hears the knock clearly. This shows that sound can travel through:
questions.a: A liquid such as water: the knock reached her ear through the water, so sound propagates through liquids as well as solids and gases.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. The material through which sound propagates is called a medium.
II. The medium through which sound propagates can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.
III. Sound can reach a listener only if the source and the listener are in the same medium.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: in Activity 10.4 the tap of spoons under water reaches a listener in the air, so the sound travels through water and then air.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When the bell jar is pumped to a near vacuum, the ringing bell can still be seen but almost no sound is heard.
Reason (R): Light can travel through vacuum, but sound needs a material medium to propagate.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: light from the bell still reaches the eye through the near vacuum, but with no medium the sound cannot propagate to the ear.

questions.q: From the activities in the chapter, give one example of sound travelling through (a) a solid and (b) a liquid.
questions.a: (a) Solid: with an ear pressed to a desk, you hear a friend knocking or scratching on the desk through the desk. (b) Liquid: two metal spoons tapped together under water in a bucket are still heard, the sound having travelled through the water.
s: (a) a knock heard through a desk with the ear pressed on it
(b) spoons tapped under water heard through the water

questions.q: True or False: 'If the spoons in Activity 10.4 touched the bottom of the bucket while they were tapped under water, the test could no longer show, on its own, that sound travels through water.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. If the spoons touched the bucket, the sound could also travel through the bucket, which is a solid, so hearing the tap would not prove the sound came through the water. That is why the activity says to tap them without touching the sides or bottom of the bucket.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the sound could then travel through the solid bucket, so the water is no longer the only path

questions.q: Say whether sound can travel through each of the following, giving a one-line reason. (a) The steel rail of a railway track. (b) Seawater. (c) The outer space around a space station.
questions.a: (a) Yes: steel is a solid, and sound travels through solids. (b) Yes: seawater is a liquid, and sound travels through liquids. (c) No: outer space is a near vacuum, and sound needs a medium to propagate.
s: (a) yes, steel is a solid medium
(b) yes, seawater is a liquid medium
(c) no, outer space is a near vacuum with no medium

questions.q: Farhan says: 'The bell jar experiment proves that sound needs air in particular. So sound cannot travel through water.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: His claim is wrong. The bell jar experiment shows that sound needs a medium; air just happened to be the only medium in the jar. The medium can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. Activity 10.4 shows that spoons tapped under water are heard, so sound does travel through water.
s: The bell jar shows sound needs a medium, and air was the only medium present
The medium can be a solid, a liquid or a gas
Evidence: spoons tapped under water are heard, so the claim is wrong

questions.q: A teacher in a village school has only a wooden desk, a bucket of water and two metal spoons. She wants to show her class how sound travels. (a) Describe a test with the desk that shows sound travels through solids. (b) Describe a test with the spoons and the bucket that shows sound travels through liquids. (c) Name one place where neither of her tests would work, and say why. (d) State what is meant by a medium, and name the medium the sound passes through in each of tests (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) A friend knocks or scratches gently on the desk while a student presses one ear to the desk and closes the other ear; the sound is heard through the desk. (b) The spoons are tapped together under water without touching the bucket; the tap is still heard, so it travelled through the water. (c) Outer space: it is a near vacuum, with no medium, and sound cannot propagate in vacuum. (d) A medium is the material through which sound propagates. In (a) the medium is the wooden desk, a solid; in (b) the sound passes through the water, a liquid, and then the air to reach the ear.
s: (a) ear pressed on the desk hears the knock: sound through a solid
(b) spoons tapped under water are heard: sound through a liquid
(c) outer space, a near vacuum with no medium, so sound cannot propagate
(d) medium = material sound propagates through; desk (solid) in (a), water then air in (b)

questions.q: After the vacuum bell jar demonstration, three students explain why the sound faded as air was pumped out. Student X: 'The bell slowly stopped ringing.' Student Y: 'The thick glass of the jar blocks sound.' Student Z: 'As the air is removed, there is less and less medium to carry the sound.' (i) Decide whether each explanation is right or wrong, using one observation from the experiment as evidence each time. (ii) State the conclusion of the experiment and use it to explain why the crew of a spacecraft cannot hear, through space, the metal panels of a damaged satellite banging together a short distance away.
questions.a: (i) X is wrong: the bell can still be seen ringing even in a near vacuum. Y is wrong: at the start, with the jar full of air, the bell was heard loudly through the same glass, and the sound returns when air is let back in. Z is right: the sound grows fainter as air is removed and returns as air is let back in, which follows the amount of medium. (ii) Conclusion: sound cannot propagate in vacuum; it needs a medium. Outer space is a near vacuum, so there is no medium between the satellite and the spacecraft, and the sound of the banging panels cannot travel across to the crew.
s: X wrong: the bell is still seen ringing
Y wrong: the bell was heard through the same glass when air was present
Z right: loudness follows the amount of air, fading and returning
Conclusion: sound needs a medium and cannot travel in vacuum
Space is a near vacuum, so the sound of the panels cannot reach the spacecraft

questions.q: In a sound wave, a region of air whose density is higher than the average density is called a:
questions.a: Compression: a region of higher density than the average; a region of lower density is a rarefaction.

questions.q: Waves that need a material medium to propagate are called:
questions.a: Mechanical waves: they cannot propagate without a material medium, and sound is one of them.

questions.q:
Match each term in column I with its meaning in column II.
Column I: 1. Compression  2. Rarefaction  3. Longitudinal wave  4. Transverse wave
Column II: (p) particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation  (q) region of lower density than the average  (r) particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation  (s) region of higher density than the average
questions.a: 1-s, 2-q, 3-r, 4-p: a compression is denser than average, a rarefaction less dense; in a longitudinal wave particles vibrate parallel to the propagation, in a transverse wave perpendicular to it.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a speaker, an electrical signal makes a cone or diaphragm vibrate, which produces sound.
Reason (R): A microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: R describes a microphone, which does the opposite job; it does not explain how a speaker turns an electrical signal into sound.

questions.q: In Activity 10.6, a metal plate is struck near a container covered with a stretched sheet on which grains are sprinkled. (a) What happens to the grains when the plate is struck harder? (b) Does the harder strike give the sound wave a larger or a smaller amplitude, and does it carry more or less energy?
questions.a: (a) The grains jump higher, because the sheet vibrates with a larger displacement. (b) A larger amplitude, and a wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy.
s: (a) the grains jump higher
(b) larger amplitude, carrying more energy

questions.q: True or False: 'A sound wave travels from east to west along a long corridor. The air particles in the corridor vibrate east-west, back and forth about their mean positions.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Sound is a longitudinal wave: the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction of propagation (here east-west) about their mean positions, without travelling with the wave.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: in a longitudinal wave particles vibrate parallel to the propagation, about their mean positions

questions.q: Give one difference between each pair. (a) A compression and a rarefaction. (b) A longitudinal wave and a transverse wave. (c) A mechanical wave and a wave that needs no medium.
questions.a: (a) A compression is a region of higher density than the average; a rarefaction is a region of lower density. (b) In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation; in a transverse wave they vibrate perpendicular to it. (c) A mechanical wave needs a material medium to propagate; a wave that needs no medium can travel through vacuum.
s: (a) compression: higher density; rarefaction: lower density than the average
(b) longitudinal: vibration parallel to propagation; transverse: perpendicular
(c) mechanical wave needs a medium; the other can travel through vacuum

questions.q: In Activity 10.6, the grains on a stretched sheet jump when a loud sound is made near the bowl, without touching it. Mohit says: 'The louder sound pushes more air particles all the way from the plate to the sheet, and those particles knock the grains up.' Test his claim.
questions.a: His claim is wrong. In a sound wave the particles of the medium do not travel with the wave; they only vibrate about their mean positions. What reaches the sheet is energy, passed on by the vibration and collisions of particles. This energy makes the sheet vibrate, and the vibrating sheet moves the grains, which shows that sound is a form of energy.
s: Particles do not travel with the wave; they vibrate about mean positions
Energy is transferred through vibrations and collisions of particles
The energy makes the sheet vibrate and moves the grains, so the claim is wrong

questions.q: At a school assembly in Lucknow, the principal speaks into a microphone on the stage. A wire carries the signal to a speaker at the back of the hall, about 30 m away, and students near the speaker hear her clearly. (a) Is the sound wave from the speaker longitudinal or transverse? In which direction do the air particles between the speaker and the students vibrate? (b) Sound is called a mechanical wave. What does this mean, and what is the medium here? (c) Do the air particles in front of the speaker travel to the students' ears? Explain what does reach them. (d) To keep out dust, a teacher suggests sealing the speaker inside a glass box with all the air pumped out. Would the students still hear the speaker? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Longitudinal: the air particles vibrate back and forth along the line from the speaker to the students, parallel to the direction in which the sound travels. (b) A mechanical wave needs a material medium to propagate; here the medium is the air in the hall. (c) No; the particles only vibrate about their mean positions. The energy carried by the sound wave reaches their ears. (d) No (or almost nothing would be heard). The speaker would still vibrate, but between it and the glass there would be a near vacuum, and sound cannot propagate in vacuum, just as in the bell jar.
s: (a) longitudinal; particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction of travel
(b) it needs a material medium; the medium is air
(c) particles only vibrate; energy reaches the ears
(d) no: the vacuum around the speaker cannot carry sound

questions.q: A piston in a long air-filled tube starts at rest and makes exactly two complete oscillations: forward, back, forward, back, and then stays at rest after its last backward motion. Reading along the tube from the region next to the piston outwards, which order of regions does it leave?
questions.a: Rarefaction, compression, rarefaction, compression: each forward push makes a compression and each backward pull a rarefaction, and the earliest region has moved farthest from the piston, so the last one formed (a rarefaction) is nearest it.

questions.q: The SI unit of the frequency of a sound wave is the:
questions.a: Hertz (Hz), which is the same as per second (s^-1).

questions.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 400 Hz. What is its time period?
questions.a: 0.0025 s: the time period is T = 1/frequency = 1/400 s = 0.0025 s.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a sound wave.
I. The distance between two consecutive troughs is its wavelength.
II. Its time period is measured in hertz.
III. On a graph of density against distance, the highest point is called the crest.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the time period is measured in seconds; hertz is the unit of frequency.

questions.q:
Match each frequency in column I with the time period of the same sound in column II.
Column I: 1. 40 Hz  2. 125 Hz  3. 800 Hz  4. 2000 Hz
Column II: (p) 0.008 s  (q) 0.0005 s  (r) 0.025 s  (s) 0.00125 s
At a fixed point in air, 100 density oscillations take place in 5 s. Find (a) the frequency of the sound and (b) its time period.
questions.a: (a) Frequency = 100 / 5 s = 20 Hz. (b) Time period = 5 s / 100 = 0.05 s (which is also 1/20 s).
s: (a) frequency = 100 / 5 = 20 Hz
(b) time period = 1/20 = 0.05 s

questions.q: True or False: 'A sound with a longer time period has a higher frequency.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Time period and frequency are inversely related (frequency = 1/T): a longer time period means a lower frequency, and a shorter time period means a higher frequency.
s: Verdict: False
Correct statement: frequency = 1/T, so a longer time period gives a lower frequency

questions.q: A graph of density against distance for a sound wave has crests at 0.4 m, 1.2 m and 2.0 m, and troughs at 0.8 m and 1.6 m. (a) What is the wavelength? (b) Name the region of the wave at 1.2 m. (c) What does the horizontal dashed line on such a graph show?
questions.a: (a) Wavelength = distance between consecutive crests = 1.2 m - 0.4 m = 0.8 m. (b) A compression (the crest, where density is highest). (c) The average density of the medium.
s: (a) wavelength = 1.2 - 0.4 = 0.8 m
(b) a compression, at the crest
(c) the average density of the medium

questions.q: In a lab, tuning fork A makes 500 vibrations in 2.5 s and tuning fork B makes 250 vibrations in 2.5 s. (a) Find the frequency and time period of the sound from each fork. (b) Which fork vibrates faster, and how does its time period compare with the other's?
questions.a: (a) A: frequency = 500 / 2.5 = 200 Hz, time period = 1/200 = 0.005 s. B: frequency = 250 / 2.5 = 100 Hz, time period = 1/100 = 0.01 s. (b) Fork A vibrates faster (twice the frequency), and its time period is half of B's (0.005 s against 0.01 s), as a higher frequency means a shorter time period.
s: Fork A: 200 Hz and 0.005 s
Fork B: 100 Hz and 0.01 s
A vibrates faster; its time period is half of B's

questions.q: Two sounds are studied at the same fixed point in air. Sound P makes 1200 density oscillations in one minute. Sound Q has a time period of 0.025 s. (a) Find the frequency of P. (b) Find the frequency of Q. (c) Which sound has the shorter time period, and by how much? (d) Arjun says: 'P has the higher frequency, because 1200 is much bigger than the 40 we got for Q.' Explain his mistake.
questions.a: (a) One minute = 60 s, so frequency of P = 1200 / 60 = 20 Hz. (b) Frequency of Q = 1 / 0.025 = 40 Hz. (c) P has time period 1/20 = 0.05 s and Q has 0.025 s, so Q's time period is shorter by 0.025 s. (d) 1200 is the number of oscillations in a minute, not per second; frequency is oscillations per unit time (per second), so P's frequency is only 20 Hz, lower than Q's 40 Hz.
s: (c) Q is shorter: 0.025 s against 0.05 s, by 0.025 s
(d) 1200 is per minute, not per second; P is 20 Hz, lower than Q

questions.q: Ria whistles three times into a phone app placed at a fixed point. The app reports the time period of each whistle: first 0.00125 s, second 0.0025 s, third 0.002 s. (i) Find the frequency of each whistle. (ii) Which whistle had the highest frequency? (iii) Ria claims the first whistle completes 48,000 oscillations in a minute. Check her claim. (iv) She also claims the frequency halved from the first whistle to the second. Check this claim. (v) Her friend says the third whistle had the longest time period. Is he right?
questions.a: (i) First: 1/0.00125 = 800 Hz; second: 1/0.0025 = 400 Hz; third: 1/0.002 = 500 Hz. (ii) The first whistle, at 800 Hz. (iii) Correct: 800 oscillations per second x 60 s = 48,000. (iv) Correct: 800 Hz to 400 Hz is half. (v) No: the second whistle had the longest time period, 0.0025 s, which matches its lowest frequency, 400 Hz.
s: (i) 800 Hz, 400 Hz and 500 Hz
(ii) the first whistle, 800 Hz
(iii) 800 x 60 = 48,000: claim correct
(iv) 800 Hz to 400 Hz is half: claim correct
(v) wrong: the second whistle (0.0025 s) had the longest period

questions.q: At a lake, a bell is rung under water 30 m from a diver, and at the same instant an identical bell is rung in the air 30 m from a boatman. Take the speed of sound as 1500 m/s in water and 340 m/s in air. Which statement is correct?
o: The diver hears his bell first, about 4 to 5 times sooner
The boatman hears his bell first, about 4 to 5 times sooner
Both hear their bells at the same instant, as the distances are equal
The diver hears his bell first, about 15 to 20 times sooner
questions.a: The diver hears his bell first, about 4 to 5 times sooner: sound takes 30 / 1500 = 0.02 s in water but 30 / 340 = about 0.088 s in air, since sound travels about 4 to 5 times faster in water than in air.

questions.q: A sound of frequency 170 Hz travels through air at 340 m/s. What is its wavelength?
questions.a: 2 m: wavelength = speed / frequency = 340 / 170 = 2 m.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sound travels faster through the air on a hot, humid day than on a cold, dry day.
Reason (R): The speed of sound in air increases as the temperature or the humidity increases.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: higher temperature and higher humidity both raise the speed of sound in air.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. A sound wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy.
II. The amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum change in density in a compression (or rarefaction) compared to the average density.
III. Sound travels about 4 to 5 times faster in air than in water.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is reversed: sound travels about 4 to 5 times faster in water than in air.

questions.q: (a) Define the intensity of sound. (b) How does the intensity change as you move away from the source?
questions.a: (a) Intensity is the amount of sound energy passing through a unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation in unit time. (b) It decreases with distance from the source, as the same energy spreads over a larger area.
s: (a) sound energy through unit area, perpendicular to propagation, per unit time
(b) it decreases with distance as the energy spreads over a larger area

questions.q: A sound wave travels through water at 1500 m/s and has a wavelength of 3 m. (a) Find its frequency. (b) The same sound passes into air, where it travels at 340 m/s. Find its wavelength in air.
questions.a: (a) Frequency = speed / wavelength = 1500 / 3 = 500 Hz. (b) The frequency is set by the source and stays 500 Hz; only the speed changes, so wavelength in air = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m.
s: (a) frequency = 1500 / 3 = 500 Hz
(b) same frequency in air: wavelength = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m

questions.q: Use Table 10.1 (speed of sound: steel 5000 m/s, water 1500 m/s, air 340 m/s). How far does sound travel in 2 s through (a) steel, (b) water and (c) air?
questions.a: Distance = speed x time. (a) Steel: 5000 x 2 = 10000 m. (b) Water: 1500 x 2 = 3000 m. (c) Air: 340 x 2 = 680 m.

questions.q: On a stage, a drum gives a low note of 85 Hz and, at the same instant, a flute gives a high note of 1700 Hz. Kunal says: 'The low note will reach the back of the 34 m hall later, because a lower frequency travels slower.' Take the speed of sound in the hall as 340 m/s. Test his claim by finding the wavelength of each note and the time each takes to cross the hall.
questions.a: His claim is wrong. In air the speed of sound depends on the medium, not on the frequency. Drum note: wavelength = 340 / 85 = 4 m; flute note: wavelength = 340 / 1700 = 0.2 m. Only the wavelength changes with frequency. Both travel at 340 m/s, so each takes 34 / 340 = 0.1 s to cross the hall and they arrive together.
s: Wavelengths: 340 / 85 = 4 m and 340 / 1700 = 0.2 m
Both take 34 / 340 = 0.1 s, so they arrive together
Claim wrong: speed in air depends on the medium, not the frequency; only the wavelength changes

questions.q: A loudspeaker plays a tone of frequency 50 Hz in air, where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Answer each part. (i) Find the wavelength of the tone in air. (ii) Find its time period. (iii) How far does the sound travel in air in 4 s? (iv) The same 50 Hz tone is sent into water, where sound travels at 1500 m/s. Find its wavelength in water. (v) In which medium is the wavelength longer, and why?
questions.a: (i) Wavelength = 340 / 50 = 6.8 m. (ii) Time period = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s. (iii) Distance = 340 x 4 = 1360 m. (iv) Wavelength in water = 1500 / 50 = 30 m. (v) In water: the frequency is the same, and since wavelength = speed / frequency, the faster speed in water gives the longer wavelength.
s: (v) water, because the same frequency at a faster speed gives a longer wavelength

questions.q: A science club in Shimla measures how long a loud clap takes to cross their 344 m long sports ground. They do it twice: once at dawn, when the dry air is at about 0 degrees Celsius (speed about 331 m/s), and once in the afternoon, when it is about 22 degrees Celsius (speed nearly 344 m/s). Their notebook shows two times, 1.04 s and 1.00 s, but they forgot to write which is which. (a) Find the time taken in the afternoon. (b) Find the time taken at dawn, to two decimal places. (c) Match each recorded time to the right session. (d) One member suggests clapping much louder at dawn so that the clap crosses the ground in 1.00 s, as in the afternoon. Would this work? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Afternoon: 344 / 344 = 1.00 s. (b) Dawn: 344 / 331 = 1.04 s (about 1.039 s). (c) 1.04 s was the dawn run and 1.00 s the afternoon run: sound is slower in colder air, so it takes longer. (d) No: the speed of sound in air depends only on the medium (here, its temperature), not on the source. A louder clap has a larger amplitude and carries more energy, so it travels farther before fading, but not faster.
s: (c) 1.04 s at dawn, 1.00 s in the afternoon, since sound is slower in colder air
(d) no: speed depends on the medium, not the source; louder means more energy, not more speed

questions.q: Sound waves with a frequency above 20 kHz are called:
questions.a: Ultrasonic waves: they are above the human audible range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz; waves below 20 Hz are infrasonic.

questions.q: According to the chapter, which of these animals can detect infrasound?
questions.a: Elephant: elephants can detect infrasound, while dogs, cats, bats and dolphins can detect ultrasound.

questions.q:
Match each term in column I with its meaning in column II.
Column I: 1. Pitch  2. Loudness  3. Timbre  4. Octave
Column II: (p) how humans perceive the amplitude of a sound wave  (q) the interval between two notes where one has double the frequency of the other  (r) how humans perceive frequency  (s) the quality that makes different instruments playing the same note sound unique
questions.a: 1-r, 2-p, 3-s, 4-q: pitch is how frequency is perceived, loudness is how amplitude is perceived, timbre makes instruments on the same note sound unique, and an octave is a doubling of frequency.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A clap cannot be heard as a clear echo from a wall 15 m away. Take the speed of sound as 340 m/s.
Reason (R): Sound takes at least 0.1 s to travel one way from a clapper to a wall 17 m away.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the echo from 15 m returns after 30 / 340 = about 0.09 s, less than 0.1 s, so it is not heard separately. But sound reaches a 17 m wall in only 17 / 340 = 0.05 s; it is the trip there and back (34 m) that takes 0.1 s.

questions.q: A ship's sonar sends an ultrasonic pulse straight down into the sea and receives the echo from the sea bed 1.2 s later. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. (a) How long does the pulse take to reach the sea bed? (b) Find the depth of the sea.
questions.a: (a) The pulse goes down and comes back, so it takes 1.2 / 2 = 0.6 s to reach the sea bed. (b) Depth = 1500 x 0.6 = 900 m.
s: (a) one-way time = 1.2 / 2 = 0.6 s

questions.q: True or False: 'A person with normal hearing can hear a sound of frequency 15 Hz.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The human audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; a 15 Hz sound is below 20 Hz, so it is infrasonic and humans cannot hear it.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: 15 Hz is below the 20 Hz lower limit, so it is infrasonic

questions.q: Sneha shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 1.5 s later. Take the speed of sound as 340 m/s. (a) Find the total distance the sound travelled. (b) Find her distance from the cliff. (c) She walks 100 m straight towards the cliff and shouts again. After how long, to two decimal places, does she hear the echo now?
questions.a: (a) Total distance = 340 x 1.5 = 510 m (to the cliff and back). (b) Distance from cliff = 510 / 2 = 255 m. (c) New distance = 255 - 100 = 155 m; the sound travels 2 x 155 = 310 m, so time = 310 / 340 = 0.91 s.

questions.q: In a large school hall with bare walls and a hard floor, speeches sound garbled because the sound seems to go on after the speaker stops. (a) Name this effect and explain its cause. (b) Suggest two changes to the hall, from the chapter, and say why they help.
questions.a: (a) Reverberation: the sound undergoes multiple reflections from the walls, and reflections arriving less than 0.05 s apart make it persist after the source stops. (b) Any two of: sound-absorbing panels, upholstered chairs, curtains or other soft, porous surfaces. These absorb sound instead of reflecting it, so fewer reflections reach the audience and the speech becomes clear.
s: (a) reverberation, caused by multiple reflections arriving less than 0.05 s apart
(b) two changes such as sound-absorbing panels, upholstered chairs or curtains
Soft, porous surfaces absorb sound and reduce unwanted reflections

questions.q: A bat flying at night in a cave sends out a short burst of ultrasonic waves of frequency 50 kHz. It receives one echo from a moth after 0.02 s and another echo from the cave wall after 0.1 s. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s. (a) Could a person standing nearby hear the bat's burst? Give a reason. (b) How far away is the moth? (c) How far away is the wall? (d) Name the ability the bat is using and explain how the two echoes tell it which object is nearer.
questions.a: (a) No: 50 kHz is above 20 kHz, the upper limit of human hearing, so it is ultrasonic. (b) Moth: 340 x 0.02 / 2 = 3.4 m. (c) Wall: 340 x 0.1 / 2 = 17 m. (d) Echolocation: locating objects by sensing reflected sound. The echo from the nearer object returns sooner, so the moth's echo (0.02 s) shows it is nearer than the wall (0.1 s).
s: (a) no, 50 kHz is above 20 kHz (ultrasonic)
(d) echolocation; the earlier echo comes from the nearer object

questions.q: A navy submarine must cross a bay by Route 1 or Route 2, and it can pass only where the sea is at least 700 m deep at every point. A survey boat sent sonar pulses straight down at three points on each route. Echo times on Route 1: 1.0 s, 1.2 s, 1.4 s. Echo times on Route 2: 2.0 s, 0.9 s, 2.4 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. The navigator says: 'Take Route 2, because its average depth is much greater.' Find the depth at each point, decide which route is safe, and evaluate the navigator's argument.
questions.a: Depth = speed x (echo time / 2). Route 1: 1500 x 0.5 = 750 m, 1500 x 0.6 = 900 m, 1500 x 0.7 = 1050 m. Route 2: 1500 x 1.0 = 1500 m, 1500 x 0.45 = 675 m, 1500 x 1.2 = 1800 m. Every point on Route 1 is at least 700 m deep, but one point on Route 2 is only 675 m. So Route 1 is the safe route. The navigator is right that Route 2's average depth is greater (1325 m against 900 m), but the rule is about every point, and the single 675 m point makes Route 2 unsafe; the average hides it.
s: Uses depth = speed x half the echo time
Decision: Route 1, as every point is at least 700 m; Route 2 has a 675 m point
Navigator wrong: the average (1325 m) hides the one point shallower than 700 m
